subject.title: Oceanside — Measure R (Oceanside Charter — Prevailing Wage & Fair Competition Measure)

text: To preserve the City’s ability to continue receiving state infrastructure funding for public works projects, shall the Oceanside City Charter be amended to conform to state laws and best practices regarding prevailing wage and fair competition, including the use of project labor agreements for City public works with mandatory provisions for taxpayer protections, transparency, and accountability in the contracting process, by amending Sections 301, 302, and 303 of the Oceanside City Charter?
This measure requires Simple Majority (50%+1) of those voting on the measure.
A “yes” vote on Measure R favors amending the Oceanside City Charter.

A “no” vote on Measure R opposes amending the Oceanside City Charter. The above statement is an impartial analysis of Measure R. If you desire a copy of the proposed City Code amendment, please call the City Clerk’s Office at (760) 435-3001 and a copy will be mailed to you at no cost. The text of Measure R can also be accessed at the following website: https://www.ci.oceanside.ca.us/government/city-clerk/elections-fair-political-practices-commission-reporting-program/current-elections.
Dated: August 14, 2026

Measure “R” was placed on the ballot by the Oceanside City Council. If approved by voters, Measure R would amend Sections 301, 302 and 303 of the Charter of the City of Oceanside (“Charter”) and align the Charter with laws governing state funding and financial assistance in support of public works projects. Specifically, Measure R would affirm prevailing wage requirements for all public works projects as defined in paragraph (1) of subdivision (d) of Section 1782 of the California Labor Code and, consistent with Public Contract Code sections 2500-2503, would affirmatively allow, but not require, the City Council to enter into or require a project labor agreement (“PLA”) for City public works projects that includes the taxpayer protection provisions of Public Contract Code section 2500.

The Charter was approved by Oceanside voters in 2010. As adopted, the Charter generally exempts the City from state laws regulating public works contracting except as provided by ordinance or by agreement approved by the City Council, limiting the requirement to pay prevailing wage and the ability to enter into public works contracts that require one or more provisions commonly associated with PLAs.

After the Charter was adopted in 2010, the California legislature passed Senate Bill 7 (SB 7) which enacted Labor Code Section 1782, and Senate Bills 922 and 829 (SB 922 & 829, respectively), which added Public Contract Code Sections 2500 through 2503. These laws generally disqualify local governments from receiving state funding for public works projects if they do not align with state laws governing prevailing wage and fair competition.

The City has maintained its qualified status for state public works funding based on interpretations that state law and the Charter can be reconciled. The City Attorney confirmed the City’s ongoing eligibility for state funding with the Department of Industrial Relations in 2014. The City pays prevailing wage on public works projects consistent with state law under the existing Charter. The City also understood that it retained the ability to enter into a PLA consistent with the Public Contract Code. PLAs are generally pre-hire agreements between a city and labor organizations containing standard terms and conditions of employment on a public works project. PLAs typically include broad prohibitions on strikes and lockouts, uniform work rules and hours, and dispute resolution protocols. Union and non-union contractors can participate in a covered project and must adhere to the PLA requirements.

Amending the Charter now aligns with state law and eliminates possible inconsistencies that generally operate to disqualify cities with charter provisions exempting prevailing wage and PLAs from receiving state funding for local infrastructure projects. If adopted, Measure R’s amendment of Sections 301, 302 and 303 would ensure the City’s continuing eligibility for state funding for infrastructure projects.
Steven Burke, Jr., City Attorney

strong: City Charter Clean Up Amendments To Protect Oceanside’s State

text: Measure R updates Oceanside’s City Charter to protect Oceanside’s fair share of state infrastructure funds for essential, local public works priorities. Measure R protects fair wages for local workers and protects taxpayers with stricter accountability. It’s a simple fix with a big impact that a bipartisan City Council majority placed on the ballot.

strong: Yes on R: Protects Oceanside From Losing Millions In State Funding

text: Oceanside adopted its charter in 2010. Since then, state laws have passed that conflict with our charter, putting Oceanside at risk of losing state funding for local public works projects. This amendment aligns our city charter with state laws to ensure Oceanside remains eligible for our fair share of state tax dollars. Other regional cities have already passed similar updates to preserve their state funding. Measure R ensures Oceanside does the same and doesn’t lose out on a single dollar.

strong: Yes on R: Protects Fair Wages & Apprenticeship Opportunities

text: Oceanside has long supported fair prevailing wage jobs for local workers that include registered apprenticeship opportunities. Measure R codifies this practice in our charter, ensuring skilled local Oceanside workers earn good wages and can afford to stay in the community they build. Measure R also allows Oceanside to expand job training and local hiring opportunities for our youth and veterans who we value greatly. In a proud military town, our veterans should always have a fair shot at reentering the workforce.

strong: Yes on R: Protects Oceanside Taxpayers

text: Measure R gives the City Council authority to establish stronger safety and taxpayer accountability protections for public works projects. Stricter accountability and oversight means city infrastructure that’s on-budget, safe and built to last.

text: The City of Oceanside claims that Measure R will ensure Oceanside is in compliance with state requirements for funding but the city is already in complete compliance and continues to qualify for State funding. Please google for more information. Measure R is unnecessary to ensure funding.

Measure R ensures the use of project labor agreements (PLAs). PLAs add regulatory burdens that only large corporations with unions can navigate. PLA’s were specifically banned by Oceanside voters in 2010 giving the city more local control rather than giving the state more control. PLAs typically cost taxpayers an extra 25-30% in project costs. Measure R will increase local taxes and exclude Oceanside contractors from local city projects. PLA’s reduce competition, increase costs and are discriminatory against a skilled workforce that chooses to work for merit-based contractors. Under Measure R, PLAs would be completely at the discretion of the city council by majority council vote of how funds are spent.

This measure will end up taking more money from your pocket, affect your family’s quality of life, and give your hard earned dollars to government projects at inflated costs. According to a recent piece in the San Diego Union Tribune, Measure R is “a gift for the unions”. Please VOTE NO on Measure R.

text: Oceanside leaders came together to place Measure R on the ballot — Councilmembers Eric Joyce, Jimmy Figueroa and Rick Robinson, and Mayor Esther Sanchez. YES on R is also endorsed by the Middle Class Taxpayers Association, San Diego Building & Construction Trades Council and the Union Veterans Council.

The facts are simple. In 2010, Oceanside’s City Charter tried to exempt city construction from paying fair prevailing wages. Since then, California passed SB7, SB922, and SB829 to take away state funding from cities that push wages down and weaken taxpayer accountability. Oceanside has always paid fair wages, but our City Charter still doesn’t match state law. Measure R fixes that, locking in these protections so our state funding is never in doubt and local workers can afford to live in the city they help build.
